title: The Accidental Hero: How Schools Come to Depend on Individuals
author: Nick Hart
summary: This article examines a pervasive and largely unexamined pattern in school improvement: the tendency for schools to build coherence through exceptional individuals rather than through systems, leaving them vulnerable when those individuals leave. Nick Hart argues that when improvement happens in schools, the story is almost always told through a few key people — the middle leader holding a department together, the pastoral leader absorbing complexity, the senior leader carrying the whole system in their head. When those people leave, coherence fades surprisingly quickly. The piece connects this to a deeper assumption embedded in school improvement planning: that if priorities are agreed and actions specified, implementation will follow — but plans always run out, and at that point interpretation takes over and the individual's judgment fills the gap. Hart argues that schools need to shift from treating coherence as something brought by particular people to building it into the structures and shared understandings of the system itself.
points: Schools routinely improve through exceptional individuals whose departure then causes coherence to fade — a pattern that reveals a structural dependency rather than genuine organizational capacity.

Interview processes for school leadership reinforce the problem by rewarding confidence, decisiveness, and personal vision rather than the ability to build systemic coherence that survives leadership transitions.

Plans always run out: at some point interpretation takes over, and when coherence is carried by individuals rather than systems, those individuals' judgment determines whether priorities stay aligned across classrooms and departments.
The purpose of a system is what it does, not what it intends to do — if the system produces hero-dependent improvement, that is the actual system regardless of what the SIP says.

The shift required is from treating coherence as something brought by particular people to building it into shared structures, mutual accountability, and distributed understanding that outlasts any individual.
quotes: On whom does your school depend? Most of us can quickly picture them and they are not always the senior leaders: the middle leader who holds a department together through force of clarity and sheer persistence; the pastoral leader who absorbs complexity before it reaches everyone else; the teacher who translates vague priorities into something workable for the rest of the team.

When schools improve rapidly, the story is frequently told through individuals. A strong headteacher; an exceptional middle leader; a team that went above and beyond. When those people leave, coherence and clarity can fade surprisingly quickly. Priorities drift. Different interpretations emerge.

These interview processes reward confidence, clarity and decisiveness. Schools look for the person who can drive improvement, bring energy or turn things around. Under pressure to improve, people naturally look for individuals capable of making that happen.

We can treat coherence as something brought by particular people rather than something built into the system itself. And if the purpose of a system is what it does, not simply what we intend it to do, then it is no wonder we need heroes to make sense of the ambiguity.

Much of school improvement planning assumes that once priorities are agreed and actions are specified, coherence will follow through implementation. But plans always run out. At some point, interpretation takes over.
People compensate for what's not on the SIP. Many school improvement plans contain actions that are ambiguous, context-dependent, or dependent on professional judgment that was never made explicit.
